Notice of Motion
3
 
It was moved by County
Councillor Maheen Kamran and seconded by County Councillor Hamish
Mills that:
 
Council notes

The importance of
engaging young people in politics and public service to ensure a
healthy, representative, and forward-looking democracy in
Lancashire
That Government
intends to lower the voting age to 16 in time for the next general
election.

Council believes:
- 
Young people deserve to have their voices heard and to influence
decisions affecting their future.
- 
Early engagement with democratic processes fosters lifelong civic
participation and stronger communities.
- 
Lancashire County Council has a responsibility to lead by example
in promoting democratic participation
Council therefore resolves to
ask Cabinet to develop a strategy to enhance young people's
involvement in democracy and politics, including:

Organising and
supporting campaigns to encourage young people to register to vote
and participate in elections
Inviting young people
to engage with council meetings
Promoting political
education and engagement, in collaboration with local educators to
introduce or enhance political and civic education
Organising events,
such as the Great Lancashire Debate, to get young people interested
in political debates and issues
Creating more
opportunities for the Youth Council and Youth Parliament
representatives to engage with the council

By taking these
steps, Lancashire County Council can become a leading local
authority in the country to actively involve young people in the
democratic process and as an investment in our
future.
 
The Motion was put to the vote
and was LOST.
 
Notice of Motion
4
 
It was moved by County
Councillor Luke Parker and seconded by County Councillor Tom Lord
that:
 
In Lancashire, we have seen
firsthand the devastating effects that drugs have on individuals,
families and communities both locally, nationally and
internationally. This Council has previously recognised the need
for additional funding, improved treatment provision, and stronger
prevention measures to mitigate these harms

In light of the recent comments by the Leader of the Green Party,
Zack Polanski, reported by the BBC that he agreed with a Kent Green
councillor, who earlier this year called for the legalisation of
all drugs, including class A drugs like heroin and crack cocaine,
the people of Lancashire deserve reassurance that national policy
developments will not increase local harm or undermine enforcement
efforts. Consequently, this Council opposes any dilution of drugs
law, including proposals from senior Green Party figures advocating
decriminalisation or regulated legalisation of certain substances,
and resolves to:

1. Instruct the Chief Executive to write to the Home Secretary,
setting out this council's

condemnation of the
views expressed by the Leader of the Green Party and their likely
impact on local authorities
opposition to any
changes to current drugs legislation which would mean legalisation
or decriminalisation of currently illicit drugs
request that local
authorities be consulted before any significant changes to national
drug legislation

2. Share that correspondence
with all Lancashire MPs and Council Leaders, requesting their
comments on the impact of legalisation and decriminalisation of
illicit drugs on Lancashire.

purpose:
A report on admission of new Partner Funds
into Local Pensions Partnership Investments.
content:
A report on admission of new Partner Funds
into Local Pensions Partnership Investments.

County Councillor Joel Tetlow
moved a report updating Full Council on the activity undertaken to
date, next steps in the process of admitting new Partner Funds, and
potential future developments and considerations arising from the
admission of new Partner Funds into the Local Pensions Partnership
Investments pool. The steps outlined within the report and the
recommendations as set out in the report were approved by the
Pension Fund Committee at its meeting on 20 February
2026.
 
Resolved: - That; 
 
(i) 
The activity undertaken to date and the next stages
in the process of demerging LPPI from Local Pensions Partnership
Limited (LPPL) and admitting new Partner Funds into the LPPI pool,
be noted.
 
(ii) 
The demerger of LPPI from LPPL, with Lancashire
County Council (LCC) becoming a shareholder in a new holding
company (TopCo), and the admission of 7 new Partner Funds into the
LPPI pool as shareholders in TopCo, be approved.
 
(iii)Authority be delegated to the
Director of Finance and Commerce (S151 Officer), in consultation
with the Director of Law and Governance and the Head of the Pension
Fund, to take all necessary steps to give effect to such approvals,
including:
 
a) 
the capital reduction of shares within LPPL from a
nominal value of £1.00 each to £0.01 each to create
distributable reserves;
b) 
the amendment of LPPL's Articles of Association to
permit a dividend in specie from LPPL to TopCo;
c) 
subscription to 1 x £1.00 "A" share (voting
share) and 2,800,000 x £1.00 "B" shares in TopCo as
contribution to the regulatory capital for the company;
d) 
the cancellation of shares in TopCo, leading to a
return of capital to Lancashire County Pension Fund and the London
Pensions Fund Authority (LPFA);
e) 
the capital reduction of shares within TopCo from a
nominal value of £1.00 each to a lower value to be confirmed
to create distributable reserves should dividends be determined to
be paid in the future; and
f) 
entering into the various resolutions and agreements
(including the Shareholders' Agreement) required to implement the
transition to TopCo.
 
(iv)Authority be delegated to the
Director of Law and Governance to review and amend LCC's
Constitution as necessary to ensure that LCC's shareholder
functions in relation to LPPL and TopCo are discharged
appropriately, in consultation with the Chair of the Pension Fund
Committee, the Section 151 Officer and Head of Pension Fund. Any
resulting updates to LCC's Constitution shall be reported to Full
Council as part of the next scheduled Constitution
update.
topline: The Full Council has decided to approve the admission of new Partner Funds into the Local Pensions Partnership Investments pool.

content:
Nic Brooks, House Project Lead, Permanence
Service, provided an overview of the House Project, explaining that
the service operated in Preston and surrounding areas, offering
supported accommodation for young people aged 16–17 as they
prepared to live independently.
 
The Board noted that young people moved into
properties as a group so they could share experiences, support each
other with challenges such as utilities and furnishing, and receive
ongoing support from a facilitator who lived alongside them during
the first year.
 
The annual AQA module was outlined to the
Board, which required young people to develop a project to benefit
the community. It was confirmed that this year the group had chosen
to organise a sponsored run on 18 April 2026 to raise funds for
Lancashire care leavers, including those involved in the House
Project and that raised funds would support activities such as
walking groups, residentials, and other opportunities to help young
people build community connections and participate in positive
experiences.
 
The Board were informed that young people had
written a script and created an animation to promote the event. The
video was in the final stages of preparation and would be
circulated across the Council via the Communications Team and would
be shared with the Board and asked that members circulate within
their areas also. A pitch had already been made to the Integrated
Care Board (NHS) to encourage wider support too.
 
Following the fund raising, it was explained
that a Microsoft Form would be created for young people and
community groups in order to request funding. A quarterly panel,
consisting of young people from the House Project and two staff
members, would review applications and allocate funds
proportionately.
 
Maddie, a young person from the House Project,
shared examples of activities young people hoped to participate in,
which included trips to the Natural History Museum, visits to the
Lake District, cinema trips, city visits, a Christmas meal, and
residential activities.
 
Following the presentation, members discussed
ideas for fundraising, which included bake sales and opportunities
to widen participation such as walks alongside the main run and
members expressed enthusiasm for supporting the awareness of the
GoFundMe campaign.
 
Members were invited to join the sponsored run
on 18 April 2026.
 
The Chair asked members to continue to
consider potential fundraising opportunities and individuals within
their networks who may be able to support and confirmed that the
GoFundMe QR code and relevant links would be circulated with the
minutes.
 
Resolved:  That the Corporate Parenting
Board:
 
(i) 
Agreed to support promotion of the GoFundMe campaign across
networks and social media platforms.
(ii) 
Agreed to share further fundraising ideas directly with Nic Brooks,
email: Nic.Brooks@lancashire.gov.uk.
topline: The Corporate Parenting Board has decided to support a fundraising campaign for Lancashire care leavers organized by young people in supported accommodation.

content:
Kirsty Clark, Project Co-ordinator, National
Youth Advocacy Service (NYAS) presented to the Board, the National
Youth Advocacy Service (NYAS) Annual Report for 2024/25, explaining
that the service was commissioned by Lancashire County Council to
deliver Advocacy and Independent Visitor (IV) services for children
in care, care leavers, and other eligible young people.
 
It was outlined to the Board that the purpose
of advocacy was to ensure young people were fully involved in
decisions affecting their lives, and that advocates supported them
to express their views, understand their rights, and influence
policy, practice and planning.
 
During 2024/25, National Youth Advocacy
Service (NYAS) received 292 advocacy referrals overall, including
those for child protection and child-in-need cases.  For the purpose of the Corporate Parenting Board,
Kirsty reported that 184 referrals during the year related
specifically to children in care and care leavers.
 
The Board noted that the most common advocacy
issues raised included:
 
· 
Living arrangements (e.g., requests to move or remain in a
placement).
· 
Relationships with social workers or Personal Advisors (PAs).
· 
Support with attending review meetings.
· 
Concerns about placement quality or stability.
· 
An increase in requests from young people wanting to submit Stage 1
complaints.
 
It was emphasised that while advocates
encouraged informal resolution, advocacy is always led by the young
person, and where they insisted on making a complaint, advocates
supported them to do so.  National Youth
Advocacy Service (NYAS) had also begun recording accommodation
types for advocacy referrals. Based on the data available, it was
reported that:
 
· 
29% were living in residential care,
· 
19% in foster care,
· 
15% in semi?independent/supportive accommodation, although it was
caveated that for some referrals the accommodation type was not
recorded.
 
The Board received a description of the
Independent Visitor (IV) service, explaining that:
 
· 
Children in care were entitled to an Independent Visitor (IV) - a
volunteer matched to them as a consistent mentor, befriender and
trusted adult.
· 
Independent Visitors (IVs) visited once a month, funded for
activities.
· 
Matches could last for many years, with some lasting up to a
decade, and often continued informally after the young person
turned 19.
 
During 2024/25, National Youth Advocacy
Services (NYAS) had 50 matched young people with Independent
Visitors (IVs), and demand for volunteers continued to exceed
availability.  Members were encouraged
to promote volunteer recruitment and offered to share posters.
Following the presentation, a number of
questions were raised as follows:
 
· 
Volunteer requirements: over 18, DBS?checked, digital risk
assessment, interview, online and live training, completion of
written exercises, and ongoing monthly reporting.
· 
Referral routes: referrals could come from social workers,
Independent Reviewing Officers (IROs), or young people
directly.
· 
Activity budget: Independent Visitors (IVs) received £30 per
visit, which included activity costs and travel.
· 
Advocacy triggers: there were no automatic referrals, but certain
situations (e.g., homelessness protocol assessments, disagreements
over plans) required practitioners to offer advocacy.
 
The Board were also informed that the KNAPPMAN
Fund, was available nationally through the National Youth Advocacy
Service (NYAS), offering up to £500 (average
£300–£350) for care leavers aged 16–25 who
had accessed National Youth Advocacy Service (NYAS) advocacy at any
point.
 
Members suggested that National Youth Advocacy
Service (NYAS) re?engage directly with Children in Care Council
(CICC)/Care Leavers Forum (CLF) sessions, and the Permanence
Service, Lancashire County Council.
 
Resolved:  That the Corporate Parenting
Board:
 
(i) 
Received and commented on the Annual Report 2024-2025.
(ii) 
Requested that National Youth Advocacy Service (NYAS) provide
responses to several outstanding questions.
(iii) 
Requested that National Youth Advocacy Service (NYAS) re-engage
with Children in Care Council and Care Leavers Forum and the
Permanence Service at Lancashire County Council.
topline: The Corporate Parenting Board has approved the recommendations in the National Youth Advocacy Service (NYAS) Annual Report for 2024/25.

content:
Claire Smith presented the young
people’s update and explained that, for the first time, young
people had received accessible summaries of Board reports in
advance, allowing discussion at the Care Leaver Forum and wider
feedback from care?experienced young people. Members were thanked
for meeting earlier deadlines, and it was noted that future reports
would continue to require young person friendly summaries, with
stricter expectations for presentation timings to allow space for
reflection after each agenda item.
 
The Board were informed that funding of
£4,700 had been secured from the Eric Wright Foundation
towards a summer residential at the Water Park in Coniston, aiming
to take 25–30 young people and offer an accredited leadership
qualification alongside outdoor activities. A small funding gap
remained, but the team were confident this would be met.
 
It was noted that work also continued on the
Welcome Box Project, supporting children on their first night in
care or during placement moves. Positive discussions had taken
place with fostering teams, and a funding application (approx.
£3,000) had been submitted to Coram Voice to produce guidance
resources created by young people.
 
The Proud Awards, held on 12 February 2026 at
Life Church Burnley, were reported as the largest to date, with
excellent feedback on the venue, performances, and food. Young
people played a central role in running the event.
 
On behalf of the Children in Care Council and
the Care Leavers Forum, Clare Smith thanked Sam Gorton for 17 years
of support to the Board and her 33 year career with the Council,
recognising her commitment and contributions ahead of her
retirement.
 
Following reflection of the presentation, it
was agreed that further funding information for young people would
be shared with the Board and is attached to these minutes.
 
Resolved:  That the Board received and
commented on the young people's update.
topline: The Council has decided to approve funding for projects supporting young people in care, including a summer residential program and the Welcome Box Project.

content:
Janice Laing, Team Manager for Children in Our
Care, and Joe Moore, Leaving Care Team Manager, Lancashire County
Council presented the Lancaster District Update, accompanied by
care?experienced young people and a Residential Child Care Worker,
Sam Cottam.
 
The Board received the presentation attached
to the Minutes, which outlined that the Lancaster district
supported 171 children in care, with 143 open to the Lancaster
teams, and 157 care leavers aged 16–25. The majority of
children resided within the Lancaster area, with most placed in
foster homes, and almost all care leavers residing in accommodation
deemed suitable under the Department for Education definitions.
 
It was also highlighted to the Board, the
team's strong participation and engagement across the district,
noting a well?established programme of co?production sessions,
walking groups, cooking workshops, a podcast series, and the Care
Leaver Forum.  Several Lancaster young
people had been finalists and winners at the recent PROUD
Awards.
 
Other work that was happening in the district,
was innovative life?story work, including culturally focused
projects designed to strengthen children’s identity and
understanding of their heritage as well as effective partnership
working with local agencies, including residential providers, the
Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), and the Employment Support
Team, contributing to improved outcomes. Joint working between the
Children in Our Care and Leaving Care teams continued to support
consistent pathway planning.
 
A number of key challenges were identified,
particularly relating to housing pressures, where Lancaster’s
dominant student accommodation market continued to limit the
availability and affordability of suitable housing options for care
leavers. It was also reported that there were difficulties in
stepping young people down from residential provision due to
limited supported accommodation and shortages in social
housing.  Work was ongoing to develop a
guarantor scheme, expand dispersed housing options, and maintain
regular joint planning meetings with district housing partners.
 
In terms of education, training and employment
(EET) this also remained a further challenge, with a higher
proportion of care leavers not engaged in education, training and
employment (EET) compared with 16–18?year?olds in care. The
Board noted that contributing factors included limited training
opportunities locally and higher numbers of care leavers unable to
work due to illness or disability, and the team continued to
prioritise earlier and more robust education, training and
employment (EET) planning and to work closely with Department for
Work and Pensions (DWP) and the Employment Support Team to improve
outcomes.
 
The care?experienced young people in
attendance at the meeting, briefly reflected on their involvement
in recent team?led activities earlier that day, noting positive
experiences of group challenges and outdoor activities, and
highlighting the sense of support and connection within the
service.
 
Following a reflection of the presentation it
was:
 
Resolved:  That the Corporate Parentig
Board:
 
(i) 
Noted the Lancaster District Update and endorsed the continuation
of participation and co?production work as a core strength of the
service.
(ii) 
Supported the ongoing development of improved housing pathways,
including the exploration of the guarantor scheme and strengthened
collaboration with district housing partners.
(iii) 
Endorsed the continued focus on Education, Employment and Training
(EET) planning, recognising the higher levels of Not in Education,
Employment or Training (NEET) among Lancaster care leavers and the
need for earlier intervention.
topline: The Corporate Parenting Board has decided to approve recommendations for the Lancaster District Update on children in care and care leavers.

content:
Heidi Fligauf, Senior Manager,
Adolescent Services, Fostering and Adoption, Lancashire County
Council presented a summary of the Fostering Service Annual Report
2024–25, highlighting key achievements, developments and
priorities for the service.  A
presentation was attached to the agenda.
 
The Board noted that Kinship
fostering remained central to maintaining family identity, while
private fostering arrangements had expanded, supporting children
who had fewer immediate family options. Mainstream foster carers
continued to form the majority of placements.
 
The Board received the
following Key Data and Performance headlines, of which there
was:
 
· 
4.5% growth in mainstream foster carers, increasing
from 357 to 373 between March 2024 and March 2025, bucking the
national trend of declining approvals.
· 
824 children were living with Lancashire foster
carers at the end of March 2025, a 6.5% increase from the previous
year. Of these, 274 children were living with kinship foster
families.
· 
Available spaces increased by 5.8%, rising from 893
to 945, improving matching and placement choice.
· 
Task?centred carer occupancy reached 91.9% at year
end.
· 
Recruitment of new foster carers rose by 13.9%,
significantly outperforming national patterns.
· 
61 kinship carers were approved within the
year.
· 
Private fostering activity increased by 51.5%, with
71 arrangements involving 68 children.
· 
18 foster carers were now offering parent?and?child
placements, with 57% of requests matched in?house.
· 
Over five years, the number of children living with
in?house foster carers increased by 16%.
 
The Board noted that these
improvements reflected greater capacity, stronger stability and
improved sufficiency across the service.
 
In terms of support for Foster
Carers, the service had expanded support mechanisms,
including:
 
· 
Mentoring Academy providing support to 47 newly
approved carers.
· 
The service’s largest-ever Family Fun Day,
attended by more than 500 children and carers.
· 
An 89% increase in foster carers using the Employee
Assistance Programme (EAP) wellbeing programme.
· 
Expanded bespoke training for carers supporting
children with complex needs or teenagers.
· 
The Pause and Reflect (PAR) model, introduced in
February 2024, enabling emergency placements to prevent unnecessary
residential admissions.
· 
77% of the Pause and Reflect (PAR) interventions
prevented disruption, supported reunification or enhanced parenting
capacity.
 
The Board noted that the future
priorities had been identified in four key areas of
focus:
 
Strengthening the fostering model
 
· 
Continued development of the Mockingbird
peer-support model.
· 
Greater support for kinship families.
· 
Developing fostering?friendly employment across
Lancashire.
· 
Increasing capacity for teenagers and larger sibling
groups.

Increasing local placement availability
 
· 
Recruitment campaigns focused on older
children.
· 
Streamlined assessment pathways.
· 
Retention work to ensure carers feel
supported.
 
Supporting staff
 
· 
Monitoring the impact of service changes on
wellbeing and workload.
· 
Ensuring staff have the tools to deliver
high?quality practice.
 
Using
data for decision?making
 
· 
Further development of Power BI
dashboards.
· 
Improving the accessibility of reports for
operational and strategic use.
 
It was noted that the service
also continued to work regionally and nationally to share best
practice and support sufficiency across the Northwest.
 
Following the presentation,
several questions were submitted by young people and answers
provided, which explained that mainstream (or
“non?connected”) carers are individuals with no prior
relationship to the child, unlike kinship carers who are relatives
or known to the family, and explained the difference between
private fostering and local authority fostering, where private
fostering involves carers approved via private fostering
arrangements, either non?profit or for?profit, whereas local
authority carers foster directly for the council.  Additional questions from young people, which were
not addressed would be responded to by Heidi Fliegauf separately
following the meeting.
 
Annie Clarkson, Senior Manager,
Adolescent Services, Fostering and Adoption, Lancashire County
Council presented a summary of the Private Fostering Annual Report
and reminded members that private fostering had been part of the
Fostering Service since 2023.  The
presentation was attached to these minutes.
 
The Board noted the definition
of private fostering in that it was a legal arrangement under the
Children Act 1989, in which a parent arranged for their child to be
cared for by someone who was not a close relative.  Close relatives were defined as grandparents,
siblings, aunts, uncles, or those related by marriage. Private
fostering arrangements must be reported when they last for more
than 28 days, and the local authority was required to visit within
7 working days, completing an assessment within 42 days. These
arrangements must then be visited every 6 weeks for the first year,
and every 12 weeks thereafter.
 
It was referenced the
historical importance of private fostering regulations, noting they
had been strengthened following the death of Victoria
Climbié, which exposed significant gaps in
oversight.  It was emphasised to the
Board, the dual role of the service: assessing suitability of
arrangements and ensuring the child’s safety and wellbeing
through ongoing visits, as well as supporting parents, carers and
linking families with wider services where needed.
 
The Board received the
following Key Data and Performance headlines, of which:
 
· 
Notifications had increased by over 51%, driven by a
strengthened communications strategy and greater referrals from
police, friends, family and neighbours.
· 
27 children were living with private foster carers
at the end of March 2025, an increase of nine children from the
previous year.
· 
Performance in completing initial and statutory
visits within required timescales rose to 94.2%, ensuring children
were seen promptly and safely.
· 
71 private fostering arrangements were active at
some point during the year, relating to 68 children, with 50 new
notifications, confirming a 51.5% increase from the previous
year.
 
In terms of outcomes for
children, supported during the year:
 
· 
33% (15 children) returned home following
intervention and family support.
· 
20% turned 16 and therefore no longer required
private fostering oversight.
· 
A further 20% achieved permanence through legal
orders such as Child Arrangements Orders or Special Guardianship
Orders.
 
It was explained to the Board
that outcomes demonstrated that private fostering support often
helped resolve difficulties at home, allowed relationships to be
repaired, and ensured appropriate long?term stability where
needed.
 
The Board noted that with
regards to communications and awareness, there was a communications
campaign which included:
 
· 
New narrated presentations.
· 
Leaflets, posters and website content.
· 
Awareness?raising events.
 
These materials increased
understanding of private fostering and encouraged more people to
report arrangements.
 
With regards to Regional
Partnership Working, the service reinstated the Pan?Lancashire
Private Fostering Working Group and expanded it to include
Westmorland & Furness and Cumberland, allowing authorities to
share good practice and deliver more consistent regional awareness.

 
The service's Future Priorities
were outlined to the Board which were:
 
· 
Strengthening private fostering practice, supported
through a three?year improvement plan.
· 
Supporting staff to maintain high?quality,
relationship?based practice.
· 
Improving data use, including expanding Power BI
dashboards to support decision-making.
· 
Developing the communications strategy, including
partnerships with the English Football League, given that academy
players often live away from home and may fall within private
fostering arrangements.
· 
Launching and reviewing the updated Private
Fostering Policy and Statement of Purpose to improve clarity for
social workers, parents, and carers.
 
Following the presentation,
discussion ensued where members noted that the number of reported
cases was likely only the “tip of the
iceberg”.  Concerns were raised
that families may feel fearful of contacting the local authority,
especially where arrangements had been made informally. This
barrier was acknowledged and reiterated the importance of
reassurance, transparency, and support?focused practice.
 
A member offered to link the
service with Lancashire FA contacts, explaining their team had
experienced developing football opportunities for young people and
could connect the Service with relevant partners involved in
academy arrangements.
 
Paul Dolan, Senior Manager,
Adolescent Services, Fostering and Adoption, Lancashire County
Council introduced the annual report to the Corporate Parenting
Board on Adoption Lancashire and Blackpool service, explaining that
Adoption Lancashire and Blackpool had been created when Lancashire
County Council and Blackpool Council joined together as a Regional
Adoption Agency (RAA) following the Department for
Education’s directive for local authorities to merge adoption
services for scale, consistency and efficiency.  The presentation provided to the Board was
circulated with the agenda.
 
It was outlined that adoption
was considered when children were unable to remain with their birth
families long-term, and that Adoption Lancashire and Blackpool had
three core functions:
 
· 
Recruiting, training and assessing
adopters.
· 
Family finding—matching children with adopters
based on children’s needs.
· 
Providing post?adoption support to children,
adopters, birth parents and adopted adults.
 
It was emphasised that Adoption
Lancashire and Blackpool followed the priorities set nationally by
Adoption England, including recruiting adopters from diverse
backgrounds, improving children’s ability to maintain
meaningful relationships with people important to them, ensuring
timely matching, and providing tailored adoption
support.
 
The Board were informed of the
performance over the last year and noted that nationally it had
been a very difficult year for adoption, as there continued to be
far fewer adopters than children needing adoption, creating
substantial challenges across the country.
 
Within Adoption Lancashire and
Blackpool, performance had been mixed:
 
· 
The service was improving its timeliness in matching
children where adopters were available.
· 
However, Adoption Lancashire and Blackpool had
experienced a period of significant staffing pressures, including
sickness, maternity leave and turnover, which had reduced their
capacity to assess prospective adopters promptly.
· 
As a result, the number of adopters available had
not kept pace with demand, leading to a widening gap between the
number of adopters needed and those available.
 
It was reported that staffing
levels were now stabilising and that the service expected improved
progress in adopter assessments in the year ahead.
 
In terms of Successes and
Service Developments, despite wider challenges, several areas of
significant progress were highlighted:
 
Expansion of Adoption Support
 
Demand for adoption support was
rising, particularly around mental health, identity and school
challenges.  Adoption Lancashire and
Blackpool had strengthened its universal offer, which now
included:
 
· 
Stay and Play (0–4 years)
· 
Tween Group (4–12 years)
· 
Teen Group (13–18 years)
· 
Parents Group
· 
Dads Group
 
It was noted that the service
had streamlined its support process, enabling adopters to access
assistance more quickly and reducing previous waiting
times.
 
Strengthening Adoption Panels
 
The Board noted reported
improvements in the quality and consistency of panel report
submissions.
 
· 
79% of reports were graded good or
higher.
· 
There had been an increase in reports graded
requiring improvement, though this was attributed to improved
grading guidance designed to support professional
development.
 
The following priorities for
the coming year were:
 
Relaunching Early Permanence (EP)
 
Adoption Lancashire and
Blackpool had once been a national leader in Early Permanence, but
numbers had declined significantly in recent years - from 14 Early
Permanence placements in 2020/21 to just one so far in
2025/26.  A new campaign was being
launched to improve awareness across teams, increase Early
Permanence recruitment, and ensure Early Permanence was considered
routinely where appropriate for children.
 
Improving Contact and “Keeping in Touch”
 
National guidance emphasised
improving safe and meaningful contact between adopted children and
their birth families.  Adoption
Lancashire and Blackpool was strengthening its approach
through:
 
· 
Faster, better management of letterbox
contact.
· 
Exploration of digital contact options.
· 
Increased consideration of safe, face?to?face
contact where appropriate.
 
Ofsted Inspection Readiness
 
Lancashire and Blackpool were
both expecting inspections in the near future.
Adoption Lancashire and Blackpool was preparing by ensuring it
could clearly articulate its strengths, areas for improvement, and
the plans in place to address them.
 
Strengthening Regional Collaboration
 
Adoption Lancashire and
Blackpool continued to work closely with the six North West
Regional Adoption Agencies (RAAs) and would expand collaborative
practice using new national government funding—particularly
around therapeutic support, adopter training and school
awareness.
 
Following the discussion,
several questions were asked from young people, which were
addressed:
 
Data
on Adoptions of Teenagers
 
Young people asked for data on
the ages of children being adopted, specifically how many teenagers
were waiting for adoption or struggling to find
adopters.  It was confirmed:
 
· 
It was a national challenge that older children,
particularly teenagers, were far less likely to be adopted, due
largely to adopter preference for younger children and explained
that Adoption Lancashire and Blackpool would provide the data
separately as requested.
 
Adoption of Teenagers by Existing Foster Carers
 
A young person asked whether
foster carers could adopt teenagers in their care long
term.  It was confirmed:
 
· 
That yes, legally foster carers could adopt a
teenager they cared for.
· 
In some cases, other legal orders (e.g., Special
Guardianship Orders) might also be appropriate, depending on the
circumstances and the young person’s
relationships.
 
Members also asked whether
adoption assessments must be completed by Social Workers, by which
it was confirmed that yes, by law, adoption assessments must be
completed by qualified social workers and in terms of addressing
staff shortages, it was explained that this was now stabilising,
and that recruitment had been successful, and performance was
expected to improve.
 
Any remaining questions from
young people would be responded to via email.
 
Resolved:  The
Corporate Parenting Board thanked the officers for their detailed
presentations and that any unanswered questions would be responded
to by officers outside of the meeting as soon as
possible.  It was further agreed that
Clare Smith would forward the young people's questions to the
relevant officers.
topline: The Corporate Parenting Board has approved recommendations to improve services for foster carers, kinship families, private foster carers, and adopters.

purpose:
Better Care Fund March Update, including the
Quarter 3 submission.
content:
Matthew Emerson, Director of Strategic and
Integrated Commissioning, Lancashire County Council, provided the
Board with a report seeking formal ratification of the 2025/26
Quarter 3 Better Care Fund (BCF) submission, which had previously
been approved by the Chair under delegated authority.
 
It was noted that a workshop held earlier in
the year had informed longer?term planning for 2026/27 and 2027/28,
and that improved alignment with neighbourhood?level delivery
remained an important future requirement.
 
The Board was informed of the following
performance Quarter 3 headlines:
 
· 
Emergency admissions: data remained unavailable for the reporting
period.
· 
Discharge delays: performance was reported as not on track due to
incomplete data returns, although Members were advised that
performance had since improved.
· 
Residential admissions: performance remained on track.
· 
Financial position: approximately 75% of the annual budget had been
spent.
· 
Increased focus was required on unpaid carers, Disabled Facilities
Grants, intermediate care, and co?production.
 
Following the presentation, discussion ensued
and members raised concerns regarding:
 
· 
The transparency and clarity of Better Care Fund budget lines,
including the use of high?level categories such as
“prevention”.
· 
Insufficient financial detail to support effective political
scrutiny.
· 
The lack of systematic collection and use of service?user
experience within reporting.
· 
Limited opportunity for innovation owing to the rigidity of
long?standing allocations within the Better Care Fund.
· 
The need for clearer accountability relating to Integrated Care
Board (ICB) contributions, particularly in light of previous
mediation.
 
The Board requested that a more detailed
breakdown of Better Care Fund expenditure be presented at a future
meeting.
 
Resolved:  That the Health and Wellbeing
Board:
 
(i) 
Formally ratified the Quarter 3 2025/26 Better Care Fund
submission.
(ii) 
Requested that officers provide at a future meeting:
 
· 
enhanced financial detail and improved clarity of budget lines;
and
· 
a further update on the position regarding Integrated Care Board
contributions.
topline: The Lancashire Health and Wellbeing Board has decided to formally ratify the 2025/26 Quarter 3 Better Care Fund submission, amidst concerns raised by members regarding transparency and financial detail.

purpose:
20mph Speed Restriction:

The purpose of the proposed extension of the 20mph speed limit on
Copp Lane, Great Eccleston is to improve the safety of motorised
and non-motorised users, mitigating against additional traffic
flows and pedestrian movements from the new housing
development.

30mph Speed Restriction

A new access is to be constructed onto Copp Lane, Elswick. In order
to reduce the speed of vehicles approaching and navigating the new
junction as well as providing additional protection for all road
users and pedestrians, it is proposed to extend the existing 30mph
speed limit.

40mph Speed Restriction

This proposal introduces a shortened extent of the 40mph speed
restriction along Copp Lane that has resulted as a consequence of
extending the 30mph by virtue of street lighting at the southern
end in Elswick and extending the 20mph speed restriction at the
northern end in Great Eccleston.

Revocation and tidy up:

This proposal seeks to revoke the existing 30mph Speed Limit Orders
on High Street, Thistleton Road, Beech Road, Ash Road, Lodge Lane
and Roseacre Road, reverting the roads back to 30mph by virtue of
street lighting. The proposal also seeks to simplify and tidy up
the existing 20mph Speed Limit Order on Chesham Street, South
Street and Leckonby Street. For both aspects there will be no
changes to the restrictions or their extents on site. Therefore,
drivers will not be subject to any changes as a result.

Consultations

May-2025 which included advertising in the local press and notices
being displayed on site. Divisional county councillors were
consulted along with the council's usual consultees and the

purpose:
Bikeability funding is
distributed annually to local highway authorities by the executive
agency Active Travel England (ATE). Grant recipients can choose to
run Bikeability training or can choose to appoint training
provider(s) to manage cycle instructors on their behalf.
 
LCC opted to appoint training
providers to deliver the training on its behalf and ran an Above
Threshold Open Procedure under Schedule 3 of the Public Contract
Regulations 2015, in 2023 to establish a multi-provider,
multi-lotted framework for the periods 2024/2025, 2025/2026,
2026/2027 and 2027/2028. The framework had an initial period of 12
months running from 1st April 2024 to 31st March 2025, with an
option to extend beyond the initial term to a maximum of a further
36 months, in tranches of 12 months.
 
LCC is exercising the
permissible option to extend the framework agreement for a period
of 12 months. The extension will run from 1st April 2026 to 31st
March 2027.
content:

multi-lotted framework for the periods 2024/2025, 2025/2026,
2026/2027 and 2027/2028. The framework had an initial period of 12
months running from 1st April 2024 to 31st March 2025, with an
option to extend beyond the initial term to a maximum of a further
36 months, in tranches of 12 months.
 
LCC is exercising the
permissible option to extend the framework agreement for a period

John Davies, Head of Service
Highways Network Management, on behalf of Matt Townsend, Director
of Highways and Transport, took a decision to extend the framework
for the Provision of Bikeability Training in Lancashire. The
extension will commence 1st April 2026 and run to
31st March 2027 as permitted in the current terms and
conditions of the framework, of which the initial periods are due
to expire 31st March 2026. The extension is complaint
with the Council Standing Orders and the Public Contract
Regulations 2015.
topline: The Director of Highways and Transport has decided to extend the framework for Bikeability Training in Lancashire.

purpose: Work programme report update
content:
The Committee received an update on the
Health and Adult Services Scrutiny Committee and Steering Group
Work Programmes.
Members were informed that the next
meeting of the Committee will take place on 22 April, at which a
joint services report on adult mental health and its integration
across other service areas will be considered. An update on the CQC
inspection action plan will also be presented at that
meeting.
The Committee was advised that, in
relation to the care home provider redesign, the Council was
seeking legal advice due to the pre-election period considerations
ahead of the forthcoming elections, which had previously been
postponed.
A question was raised regarding
any update on the vascular services reconfiguration. It was
confirmed that no update had been received. However, it was noted
that no changes could be implemented until a full public
consultation has been undertaken, and that the Committee continued
to seek oversight of this process. No further updates have been
received on any of the service changes previously recommended for
consultation.
 
Resolved:
That the information provided as part of the report
be reviewed.
topline: The Health and Adult Services Scrutiny Committee has decided to review recommendations for adult mental health integration and care home provider redesign.

suitably qualified and experienced service providers, offering a
variety of staff benefit schemes

communication and marketing schemes. The benefits are offered at a
competitive rate and provide reasonable value for money to

service, it was recommended that the contract is extended for
further 12 months, utilizing the second possible extension
period.

decision_maker: Executive Director of Education and Children's Services
purpose:
A waiver of procurement rules is requested to
enable the urgent purchase of evidence-based curriculum programme
frameworks, required for delivering the Best Start in Life Strategy
in Lancashire. Government guidance specifies a restricted list of
approved programmes, and the associated grant must be spent
exclusively on these products. The implementation timeframe is
extremely limited (less than three months), and only a small number
of providers are available who meet both Lancashire’s
curriculum development needs and the constraints of the
government’s approved list.
Given these factors, following standard procurement processes would
be impractical and would significantly delay or jeopardise delivery
of this essential programme, against which we will be measured on
targets for improving the percentage of children reaching a good
level of development by the end of their reception year at school.
In such circumstances, a waiver is both necessary and justified.
This report sets out the evidence and reasons supporting the
request, and reflects advice sought from council procurement
specialists, alongside consideration of all other procurement
options, which have been assessed as either exhausted or
unviable.
content:
The Head of Service Early Help,
on behalf of the Director of Education and Inclusion,
Director of Finance and Commerce (s151 Officer),
Director of Law and Governance, Director of Education and
Inclusion, took a decision to waiver
procurement rules in relation to securing the urgent purchase of
certain evidence-based curriculum programme frameworks, required
for delivering the Best Start in Life Strategy in
Lancashire.
topline: The Executive Director of Education and Children's Services has decided to waive procurement rules for the urgent purchase of curriculum programme frameworks in Lancashire.

decision_maker: Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
A report explaining current levels of school
attendance and how we're supporting schools to improve.
content:
The Chair welcomed County Councillor Matthew
Salter, Cabinet Member for Education and Skills and Aby Hardy, Head
of Education Improvement to the meeting.
 
The report detailed the current levels of
school attendance across Lancashire and how the county council was
supporting schools to improve school attendance. It was explained
that every Lancashire school had a dedicated Attendance Support
Worker who provided termly visits and advice. An attendance toolkit
for schools was launched in 2025 and offered resources for
graduated, support first approaches, a further toolkit was being
drafted to support parents with a range of tools and advice to help
support good attendance in school. New staff recruited from April
2026 would also enhance attendance service capacity and review
frequency. 
 
The Chair invited questions and comments from
the committee, and a summary is outlined below:
 

The committee enquired about penalty
notices issued to parents when their child missed school, whether
the income was retained by the council, and whether it was felt
prosecution was a proportionate penalty. Officers advised that
approximately £1m was raised last year, which was retained
and was used to fund Attendance Staff and Children Missing
Education Staff. Decisions to issue penalty notices were made by
schools, in line with DfE guidance, with the council acting as the
issuing authority; most notices related to term?time holidays.
Members were advised that enforcement was considered as a last
resort but formed part of the wider approach to supporting
consistent attendance, with prosecutions undertaken in accordance
with national guidance.

 

Members queried the level of control
or influence the council had over school absence penalty notices
and whether advise was issued schools. Officers confirmed that the
council did provide advice to schools, but this was aligned with
Department for Education (DfE) statutory guidance.

 

The committee raised concern that
attendance discussions often focused on returning children to
school, even where mainstream provision may not be suitable.
Officers confirmed that Section 19 arrangements were used when
school was not the right place for a child at that time. This
arrangement allowed schools to work with the local authority to
access alternative education options, including individual or
small?group tuition, provision in community settings such as
libraries or placement in alternative provision or a different
educational setting. Officers explained that Section 19 provides
access to local authority funding, encouraging schools to consider
flexible solutions rather than relying solely on attendance
enforcement. The committee requested, where possible figures on the
number of children accessing alternative provision, due to
difficulties attending school and a list of alternative provision
providers.

 

The Committee discussed attendance
data which showed patterns contrary to expectations, with Preston
performing strongly while Lancaster and Ribble Valley recorded
lower attendance rates. Members queried the underlying factors,
including school type, levels of academisation, deprivation,
rurality, transport challenges, and the measurement of attendance.
Officers noted that performance in Lancaster and Ribble Valley had
improved in the autumn term but highlighted possible complexities
could include long travel distances, particularly to grammar
schools, and weaker engagement mechanisms with academies. The
Committee requested further analysis focused on Lancaster and
Ribble Valley and for a briefing note / report to come back to the
committee to look at this issue in more depth, in particular the
following areas to be considered:

Autumn?term data,
factors driving persistent
absence,
the significant increase in absence
between primary and secondary, in particular
in Ribble Valley and;
the distance children need to travel
to get to school, and if this could be a factor.



 
Resolved: That the following
recommendations be shared with the Cabinet Member for Education and
Skills:
 

That where available,
date be provided on the number of children accessing Alternative
Provision, due to attendance difficulties.

 

That a list of
Alternative Provision providers to be provided to the
committee.

 

That a report / briefing note come
back to the committee providing deeper analysis of attendance
issues in Lancaster and Ribble Valley. Consideration be given to:

Autumn?term data,
factors driving persistent
absence,
the significant increase in absence
between primary and secondary, in particular
in Ribble Valley and;
the distance children need to travel
to get to school, and if this could be a factor.
topline: The Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for improving school attendance levels in Lancashire

decision_maker: Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
This report discusses all cohorts of children
not in school including discussion around exclusion
content:
The Chair welcomed County Councillor Matthew
Salter, Cabinet Member for Education and Skills and Aby Hardy, Head
of Education Improvement to the meeting.
The Cabinet Member noted the increasing trends
in children missing education, elective home education and
education otherwise than at school. While acknowledging that
elective home education can be positive where provision is of good
quality, it was noted that rising numbers may possibly reflect
wider issues, including SEND challenges and disengagement with the
education system, and there was a need to strengthen support to
re?engage families and enable children to return to school, where
appropriate.
 
The Chair invited questions and comments from
the committee, and a summary is outlined below:
 

Members queried whether statutory
School Attendance Orders had increased and the associated
timescales. It was confirmed that orders have risen in line with
increased Children Missing Education (CME) referrals, but capacity
had remained the same, although this was now being addressed, and
the process remained lengthy, often taking several months due to
appeals and complexities, including challenges in securing suitable
school placements and cases where families provide further evidence
to continue home education.

 

Members expressed concern about the
high number of CME in Preston and other areas and requested further
detail on the length of time children were waiting for school
places, the reasons behind cases, and a breakdown by district,
primary and secondary places and distance travelled. Officers
advised that CME numbers were broadly split between primary and
secondary pupils, with higher numbers in Years 10–11, largely
linked to Elective Home Education (EHE) returns, often associated
with exam pressures. It was noted that some cases also reflected
new arrivals into the area, and other key factors for high EHE
numbers included mental health needs and perceptions that schools
cannot meet pupils’ needs, rather than relationship
breakdowns with the school. It was noted that most EHE families
reported positive engagement with the authority, capacity
challenges have existed; improvements were being made through
increased staffing from three to five team members and earlier
intervention. A dedicated phone line for the EHE Team has been
introduced to support both schools and parents in making informed
decisions.

 

Members questioned what actions were
being taken to reduce the numbers of CME, particularly in areas
such as Preston, Hyndburn and Ribble Valley. Officers advised that
further analysis was being undertaken to better understand the
specific drivers in high?demand areas, noting that population
movement in places like Preston could be a significant factor.
Operationally, capacity had been increased within the CME Team,
with additional staffing and a revised approach whereby officers
now retained cases throughout, supporting families until school
places were secured. Additional work was ongoing through Fair
Access Protocols to reduce delays, improve school responsiveness,
and promote a more inclusive culture, including the use of powers
to direct placements where necessary.

 

Further to the above discussion, it
was agreed that the committee would be provided with a breakdown of
figures for Children Missing Education (179 in Preston and 101 in
Hyndburn/Ribble Valley) to provide further detailed
analysis including the length of time out of education, primary and
secondary breakdown, contributing factors, and the possible impact
of travel, distance and transport accessibility. Where possible,
details would be provided about what was being done to specifically
bring down these numbers.

 

The committee queried how it was
determined whether EHE was effective for individual families, and
whether further information was sought from schools to better
understand the reasons behind a family’s decision,
particularly where the school’s account may differ. Officers
advised that suitability was assessed against guidance, including
the expectation of a full-time education (around 25 hours),
provision of literacy and numeracy, and evidence that the child was
making appropriate progress, taking account of any special
educational needs. Alongside working directly with families, the
council analysed patterns in referrals and engaged termly with
schools that have higher numbers of EHE cases to better understand
underlying causes, recognising that accounts from families and
schools can differ and are explored further where needed.

 

It was queried what plans were being
considered to provide additional support for home educated families
and to address issues arising from unmet SEND needs. Officers
advised that work was underway to improve inclusive practice across
schools through the SEND improvement programme, focusing on earlier
identification and support to prevent escalation. Increased
capacity within the EHE Team would also enable more direct support,
including the development of support groups, alongside closer
working with Family Hubs to offer localised support, improve access
to services, and strengthen engagement with families.

 

Members highlighted the role of
colleges in supporting young people, particularly those
transitioning from home education or at risk of becoming NEET, and
raised concerns about funding constraints affecting provision,
especially for 14–15-year-olds. It was noted that while some
colleges offer early access programmes, these are often limited due
to funding arrangements, with variation across areas. It was
suggested by Members that a visit be arranged to one of the
colleges to better understand current provision, including
progression pathways for 14-15 year olds.

 

Members raised concerns about the
potential criminalisation of families where children are not
attending school due to mental health needs, and whether this could
influence decisions to electively home educate. Officers clarified
that families who elect to home educate and provide suitable
education are not subject to fines or prosecution. Enforcement
action in relation to non-attendance followed a graduated response,
with fines or prosecutions used only as a last resort where there
has been persistent non-engagement with support. It was
acknowledged that messaging around enforcement may sometimes be
misinterpreted, and this would be reviewed if specific concerns are
identified.

 

Members requested further analysis
of the increase in CME, including clearer data on trends over time,
inflow and outflow of cases, and whether this reflected local or
national patterns. Officers advised that post-COVID increases, and
greater population movement had contributed nationally and agreed
to provide more detailed breakdowns. Members suggested the
establishment of a forum for home educating families to better
understand their needs, which officers confirmed was being
explored. Concerns were also raised about the potential for
off-rolling; officers reiterated this was unlawful and challenged
where identified, noting that most cases of pupils leaving in Years
10–11 were linked to exam pressures and mental health rather
than school practices.

 

Members queried how the council
fulfilled its statutory duty to ensure suitable education for
home-educated children, given that contact may only occur annually.
Officers explained that current guidance only required families to
provide annual updates, which the council must accept unless there
were safeguarding concerns or other known issues, in which case
more proactive engagement may take place. Assessment of progress
was undertaken where appropriate by reviewing evidence of a
child’s development over time; however, for most families,
the council relied on parental assurance due to limited legal
powers to intervene.

 
Resolved: That the following recommendations be shared with the
Cabinet Member for Education and Skills:
 

That a breakdown of figures for
Children Missing Education (179 in Preston and 101 in
Hyndburn/Ribble Valley) be provided to the committee to provide
further detailed analysis including the length of
time out of education, primary and secondary breakdown,
contributing factors, and the possible impact of travel, distance
and transport accessibility. Where possible, details to be provided
about what is being done to specifically bring down these
numbers.

 

That consideration be given for a
member visit to be arranged to Burnley College or possibly
Lancaster and Morecambe College, to enhance members’
understanding of NEET provision, including progression pathways for
14–15-year-olds.

 

That regarding Data
for Children not in School (CME Referrals and EHE numbers), further
contextual (graphical and numerical) data be provided to
illustrate trends over time, to allow for consideration of
both pre and post COVID trends. Analysis could include:

Flow data showing the number of
children entering and leaving CME over time.
Possible RAG-rated analysis breaking
down the figures.
Comparison with
national trends, including analysis of how local patterns align
with or diverge from post-COVID national data.



 

That officers explore
the establishment of a Home Education Forum or engagement mechanism
to improve communication and understanding with children who are
home educated and their parents, to support partnership working and
early identification of emerging issues and provide progress
updates to the committee when possible.
topline: The Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee has decided to address the increasing trends in children missing education and elective home education by approving recommendations for further analysis and support initiatives.

purpose:
This report explains how we calculate need for
school places and the current forecasts
content:
The Chair welcomed County Councillor Matthew
Salter, Cabinet Member for Education and Skills and Aby Hardy, Head
of Education Improvement to the meeting.
 
The report explained how the service
calculated need for school places and the current forecasts. The
committee were informed that the council had a legal duty to ensure
that every child had school place. Officers highlighted that in
some areas there was now surplus school places across Lancashire,
reflecting a national decline in birth rates and reduced pupil
numbers. Work was underway to develop a Surplus Places Strategy in
collaboration with partners, with proposals for it to come back to
scrutiny in the future.
 
The Chair invited questions and comments from
the committee, a summary is outlined below:
 

A Member queried the prioritisation
of out-of-area and SEND applications. Officers advised that
admissions follow the Council’s policy agreed in February,
with priority generally given to children living within the local
area and to looked-after children, while SEND is not consistently
included within all schools’ criteria.

 

Members raised concerns about the
impact of new housing developments on access to school places and
the need for planning to better reflect community needs, including
travel and family considerations such as siblings attending the
same school. Officers advised that school place planning involved
balancing multiple factors, including demand, available capacity
and site constraints, and suggested that concerns regarding
admissions arrangements and local pressures should be reviewed
outside of the meeting.

 

Members queried the potential
implications of increased federation of schools, including whether
shared teaching models could result in additional transport costs
for pupils. Officers advised that current practice typically
involved sharing leadership rather than teaching staff, and where
joint teaching arrangements existed, it was teachers that would
travel between sites rather than pupils, with such models not
commonly in place, but possibly to be considered as part of future
planning in line with the Surplus Place Strategy.

 
Resolved: That the following recommendations be shared with the
Cabinet Member for Education and Skills:
 
i. 
That the draft Surplus Place Strategy come back to the scrutiny
committee once ready in the coming months, as suggested by
officers.
topline: The Children, Families and Skills Scrutiny Committee has decided to develop a Surplus Place Strategy to address the need for school places in Lancashire.

purpose:
As set out in Appendix C of the 2025/26
Maintenance of Highways Assets approved by Cabinet on 7 March, a
budget allocation of £500,000 was approved for Coring and
Surveying (PPMS16461) to support pavement design development for
the 2026/27 Highways Maintenance Programme.
We are now forecasting an underspend against this allocation. This
is due to several factors, most notably a reduction in activity
associated with the Local Deterioration Fund (LDF), which has
correspondingly reduced the level of coring and survey work
required during the current financial year.
Conversely, there has been an increased demand for Geotechnical
Investigation and Design (PPMS16464). This pressure is driven by an
extensive programme of Special Schemes, many of which involve full
pavement reconstruction and require more complex ground
investigation work. Several of these schemes have also attracted
significant public and political attention, increasing the need for
robust geotechnical assessment and design.
The originally approved budget provision for PPMS16464 was
£200,000. To support delivery of the 2025/26 programme, this
now needs to be increased by £50,000 to £250,000.
It is recommended therefore that the transfer of £50,000 from
the coring budget to the Geotechnical Investigation budget is
approved.

purpose:
Seeking support from Pensions Committee before
Full Council approve the admission of new Partner Funds to Local
Pensions Partnership Investment.
content:
The Head of Fund presented a
detailed report on the proposed process for Local Pensions
Partnership Investments Ltd (LPPI) to demerge from Local Pensions
Partnership Limited (LPPL) and become the subsidiary of a new
holding company (currently referred to as "TopCo") with Lancashire County Council, the London
Pension Fund Authority (LPFA) and 7 new Partner Funds as equal
shareholders.
 
It was also reported that the
County Council and LPFA would continue as shareholders for LPPL and
its remaining subsidiary Local Pensions Partnership Administration
Ltd which would continue to provide pension administration services
to its existing clients.
 
The Committee considered the
various stages set out in the report required for the demerger and
the establishment of the new holding company to oversee the
expanded pool and the Head of Fund and the Chief Legal and
Compliance Officer from LPPl answered
questions from Committee members. The Committee was also informed
that external legal and tax advice had been sought in relation to
the proposed demerger and admission of new Partner
Funds.
 
Resolved:
 
1.  That the
Committee:
 
a)  note the activity
undertaken to date and the next stages in the process
of demerging Local Pensions Partnership Investments Limited (LPPI)
from Local Pensions Partnership Limited (LPPL) and admitting new
Partner Funds into the LPPI pool.
 
b)  approve a dividend
in specie as set out in the report to facilitate the
demerger of LPPI from LPPL to a new holding company, ("TopCo") subject to the agreement of Full Council on
12 March 2026 to amend the Articles of Association of LPPL to
permit the payment of such a dividend.
 
c)  delegate authority
to the Director of Finance and Commerce (S151
Officer), in consultation with the Monitoring Officer and the Head
of the Pension Fund, to take all necessary steps to implement the
dividend in specie referred to in b) above.
 
d)  note the future
developments arising from the admission of new Partner
Funds into the expanded LPPI pool, as set out in the report
presented, including in relation to internal governance.
 
2.  That the Committee
recommend Full Council be asked to:
 
a)  approve the demerger
of Local Pensions Partnership Investments
Limited (LPPI) from Local Pensions Partnership Limited (LPPL), with
Lancashire County Council becoming a shareholder in a new holding
company (TopCo), and the admission of 7
new Partner Funds into the LPPI pool as equal shareholders in
TopCo.
 
b) 
delegate authority to the Director of Finance and Commerce
(S151
Officer), in consultation with the Monitoring Officer and the Head
of the Pension Fund, to take all necessary steps to give effect to
such approvals, including:
 
i.  the capital
reduction of shares within LPPL 
as set out in the report to create distributable
reserves.

ii.  the amendment
of LPPL's Articles of Association to permit a
dividend in specie from LPPL to TopCo,
as set out in the report.
 
iii. 
subscription to the amounts of "A" share (voting share) and
"B"
shares in TopCo set out in the report
as contribution to the regulatory capital for the
company.
 
iv. 
the cancellation of an amount of shares
in TopCo, leading to a
return of capital to the Lancashire County Pension Fund and London
Pensions Fund Authority (LPFA) as set out in the report.
 
v.  the
capital reduction of shares within TopCo from a nominal
value to a lower value to be confirmed to create distributable
reserves should dividends be determined to be paid in the future;
and
 
vi. 
entering into the various resolutions and agreements
(including
the Shareholders' Agreement) required to implement the transition
to TopCo.
 
c) 
Note that a review of the internal governance arrangements
regarding
certain shareholder matters is currently underway and a further
report on the outcome of the review will be presented to Full
Council in due course.
topline: The Pension Fund Committee has decided to approve the demerger of Local Pensions Partnership Investments Ltd and the establishment of a new holding company with multiple shareholders.

decision_maker: Community, Cultural, and Corporate Services Scrutiny Committee
purpose:
HR update on workforce planning to the
committee
content:
Jacquie McGeachie,
Interim Director of People Service, Deborah Barrow, Head of People
Strategy and CC Ged Mirfin, Cabinet Member for Resources, HR, and
Property were welcomed to the meeting.
 
Members were provided with an outline of
the report provided as part of the agenda pack through a
presentation drawing out key points. Context was set on the
concurrent change pressures, the efficiency plan, the improvement
plan, and the Local Government Reorganisation.
 
With regard to the Local Government
Reorganisation, members were informed that market volatility had
been anticipated, given multiple councils undergoing Local
Government Reorganisation.
 
Members were provided with some key
workforce metrics:

 

· 
On staffing, it was
reported that the establishment stood at 15,552, whilst headcount
was at 13,620, leaving approximately 1,500 vacancies.

· 
Turnover of staff
remained slightly high.

· 
Absence was
increasing, with additional support being planned.

· 
On length of service,
it was highlighted that around 5,000 colleagues had over 10
years’ service.

· 
Significant investment
was underway for apprenticeships and early careers.

 
Regarding key priorities, members were
advised that these included TUPE compliance, disaggregation
modelling, cultural considerations, wellbeing, Local Government
Reorganisation, and ensuring 'day one' readiness for all
staff.
 
Members were invited
to ask questions and a summary of discussion outlined below:
 
Members raised concerns relating to the
significant proportion of staff who had served fewer than five
years, noting the risk of losing institutional knowledge during the
transition to new unitary structures. It was explained that
modelling work had already commenced to identify which roles would
be required in successor authorities and that clarity would be
provided as early as possible. Senior level roles were expected to
face the greatest challenge, and principles relating to workforce
stability and TUPE regulations would guide future decisions.

Further discussion took place on succession planning and
opportunities for staff to progress within the new structures. It
was confirmed that workforce planning was a key priority and that
the extended lead-in period provided a valuable opportunity to
identify and support emerging talent across the organisation.

Members expressed concerns regarding the capacity required to
manage the significant workload associated with Local Government
Reorganisation. It was stated that resources would be allocated
appropriately, and additional support would therefore be required
across several council services.

The committee also discussed risks relating to specialist roles,
including social care teams and statutory positions. It was
emphasised to members the importance of preserving continuity for
vulnerable service users and acknowledged the complexity of
creating new structures without disrupting long-standing
relationships between practitioners and clients.

Members queried variations in team manager numbers and the
distinction between positions and employees. Members were advised
that the figures reflected increasing workforce demands and the
expansion of specialist roles within the organisation. Temporary
senior arrangements were highlighted as an area requiring
stabilisation prior to Local Government Reorganisation.

The committee received an update on staff survey results, noting a
decline in response rate. This was attributed partly to unusually
high participation in the previous year and indicated that levels
remained consistent with sector norms. Survey responses continued
to highlight concerns relating to change management and
communication, and officers outlined ongoing work to improve
engagement, including staff panels and leadership visibility across
services.

Members explored issues relating to hybrid working policies, staff
confidence in the reorganisation process, and the risk of councils
competing for talent. These concerns were acknowledged and
confirmed that principles for engagement with the 14 other affected
authorities would be developed. They also noted that concerns among
the workforce were linked to uncertainty rather than confirmed
outcomes, and that future updates would be provided as more
information became available.
 
Resolved: That;
 

A future report be provided detailing the
actions following item be brought forward containing a detailed
analysis of the staff survey results, including key themes,
strengths, and challenges.

 

A future report be provided to a future
meeting of the committee on the council’s hybrid working
arrangements and home working policy and its impact on retention,
morale, and service delivery.

 

A future report on the workforce matters
of Local Government Reorganisation be presented to a future meeting
of the committee, anticipated to be in Autumn 2026.  Regular
updates from the People Service to then be scheduled following key
milestones in the Local Government Review process, including a
report following the Government’s decision on the final
model.  The report to set out the planning and key milestones
of the implementation process.
topline: The Community, Cultural, and Corporate Services Scrutiny Committee has approved recommendations for workforce matters in preparation for Local Government Reorganisation.

purpose:
In November 2024, the county council was
notified of structural defects in schools constructed under the
Government’s Building Schools for the Future (BSF) Programme.
Structural engineers advised that further investigation was
required, and until these investigations and any subsequent
remedial works were completed, exclusion zones must remain in place
to ensure the continued safe operation of the schools.

Due to the failure on the part of the PFI Project Companies to take
the required action within an acceptable timeframe, pursuant to a
decision of the Interim Director of Finance and Commercialisation,
the council exercised its contractual step-in rights and arranged
for the installation of Heras fencing around all identified risk
areas, supported by on site security to ensure that no unauthorised
access occurred behind the exclusion zones.

In accordance with the Project Agreements, the associated costs are
being recovered from the PFI Contractors by way of an adjustment to
the Monthly Unitary Payments.

While a definitive timeframe for removing the exclusion zones and
security cannot yet be confirmed, the PFI Contractors have made
progress on the required remedial works, and a phased removal of
fencing and security is anticipated throughout 2026.

Additional funding is now required to secure the ongoing provision
of these arrangements until such time as time as the issues with
the masonry walls are satisfactorily remediated or satisfactory
evidence is provided that they are no longer required.
